name: Al-Ḥashr
meaning: The Gathering, The Exile, or The Banishment (derived from the word Al-Hashr in the second verse).
revelation_details: Madinan. Revealed in the 4th year after the Hijrah (migration to Madinah), following the expulsion of the Jewish tribe of Banu Nadir.
core_theme: Allah's absolute sovereignty, the consequence of treachery and treaty-breaking, the spiritual qualities of the true companions (Muhajirun and Ansar), the psychological exposing of the hypocrites, the weight of the Quran, and the majestic attributes of God.
name_origin:
The title Al-Hashr is deeply tied to the historical fate of the Jewish tribe of Banu Nadir in Madinah.

The First Gathering (Li-awwali al-Hashr)

The Surah is named after its second verse:

• "He it is Who drove out the disbelievers among the People of the Scripture from their homes at the first gathering (li-awwali al-hashr)..."* (Verse 2)

In classical Arabic, Hashr means to gather a group of people and move them collectively for a specific purpose (such as mobilization or expulsion). This event marked the very first time in Islamic history that an entire hostile tribe was gathered and exiled from the Madinan territory, relocating to places like Khaybar and Syria.

"Surah Bani an-Nadir"

The connection between the Surah and this historical event is so absolute that the companions of the Prophet (pbuh) often referred to the Surah by the tribe's name.

• Hadith Context:* Sa'id bin Jubayr narrated: "I asked Abdullah ibn Abbas (ra) about Surat Al-Hashr. He replied: 'Say, it is Surah Bani an-Nadir.'" (Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim)*

Ibn Abbas (ra) emphasized this alternative name to ensure that future generations of Muslims understood that every single verse of this Surah was tied to the lessons, events, and consequences of the campaign against the Banu Nadir.

verse_breakdowns.section_title: The Fall of the Fortresses and Divine Sovereignty
verse_breakdowns.content_markdown:
The Surah opens with a declaration of cosmic praise: "Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth exalts Allah, and He is the All-Mighty, the All-Wise." Allah then details the historical expulsion of the treacherous tribe of Banu Nadir from their fortified settlements in Medina.
The disbelievers believed their massive, stone fortresses (Husun) would protect them from Allah, but the divine decree reached them from where they least expected. Allah cast terror (Ru'b) into their hearts, leading them to destroy their own homes with their own hands and the hands of the believers. Allah clarifies that this exile was already decreed, and in the Hereafter, a far worse punishment awaits them. He also justifies the tactical cutting or sparing of their palm trees as a targeted humiliation for the defiant.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: The physical fortresses of Banu Nadir represent a psychological trap that many modern humans still fall into - the illusion that material security, wealth, and physical walls can lock out the decree of God. True security is never physical; it is spiritual. When Allah wills a change, the very structures built for protection can become the instruments of a person's ruin. The transition of their homes from sanctuaries to rubble, destroyed "by their own hands," is a stark warning to look beyond material causes to the ultimate Source of power.

verse_breakdowns.section_title: The Ethics of Wealth Distribution and the Trinity of the Ummah

points.label: The Successors
points.detail: Those who came after them, praying: "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and put not in our hearts any resentment (Ghill) toward those who have believed.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown:
Allah establishes the legal and ethical framework for Fai' - wealth acquired from an enemy without active military combat. Unlike standard spoils of war (Ghanimah), Fai' belongs entirely to Allah, His Messenger, the Prophet's family, orphans, the needy, and the stranded traveler. Allah reveals the profound socioeconomic objective of this law: "...so that it may not circulate exclusively among the rich among you."
Allah then outlines the three historical tiers of the Muslim community that are entitled to this care:
1. The Poor Emigrants (Muhajirun): Those who were expelled from their homes and wealth, seeking bounty and pleasure from Allah, and supporting Him and His Messenger.
2. The Helpers (Ansar): Those who settled in Medina and embraced faith before them. They love those who emigrated to them, find no jealousy in their hearts for what the emigrants were given, and practice extreme selflessness (I'thār) - giving preference to others even when they themselves are in desperate poverty.
3. The Successors: Those who came after them, praying: "Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith, and put not in our hearts any resentment (Ghill) toward those who have believed.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: This passage is a masterpiece of economic and social psychology. By declaring that wealth must not become a closed loop among the wealthy, Islam establishes a mandate against hyper-capitalism and systemic financial inequality. Furthermore, the description of the Ansar introduces the peak of human emotional maturity: I'thār (altruism). To be free of envy and to actively give away what you desperately need yourself is the ultimate cure for the disease of hoarding. The final prayer of the succeeding generations acts as a spiritual glue, ensuring that no historical resentment (Ghill) breaks the sacred brotherhood across space and time.

verse_breakdowns.section_title: The False Alliances and the Parable of Satan
verse_breakdowns.content_markdown:
Allah exposes the secret political maneuvers of the hypocrites (Munafiqun) in Medina, who whispered false promises of solidarity to the hostile People of the Book: "If you are expelled, we will surely go out with you... and if you are fought, we will surely aid you."
Allah exposes their cowardice with absolute certainty: if the hostile tribes are expelled, the hypocrites will not go with them; if they are fought, they will not aid them; and even if they did attempt to help, they would soon turn their backs in retreat. They fear the believers far more than they fear Allah because they are a people devoid of deep understanding. They cannot even fight the believers united except within fortified towns or from behind high walls. Their internal enmity is fierce - they appear unified, but their hearts are completely scattered (Qulubuhum Shatta). Their deception is likened to Satan, who coaxes man to disbelieve, but the moment man submits to ruin, Satan declares: "Indeed, I am disassociated from you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Hypocrisy is inherently fragile because it is built on temporary political convenience rather than shared moral principles. The description "their assemblies are united, but their hearts are scattered" perfectly diagnoses many modern coalitions, organizations, and families that look unified on paper but are internally fractured by ego and distrust. The comparison to Satan's betrayal is a chilling psychological warning: those who encourage you to cross moral boundaries for their benefit will be the very first to abandon you and claim self-righteous innocence when the consequences arrive.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Allah issues an urgent spiritual command to those who believe: "Fear Allah, and let every soul look to what it has put forward for tomorrow." He warns the believers not to be like those who forgot Allah, which led to a terrifying psychological state: "...so He made them forget themselves." These are the truly rebellious, and the inhabitants of the Fire and the companions of Paradise can never be equal.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: Verse 18 is the foundational text for Muhasabah (mindful self-auditing). Just as a successful business audits its balance sheets daily, a believer must actively audit their actions, asking: What have I sent ahead for my future? The consequence of neglecting this audit is "self-oblivion." When a person forgets their Creator, they lose their moral compass, their existential anchor, and ultimately, their very identity. They become strangers to their own souls, chasing shallow distractions while their true spiritual selves starve.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown: Allah presents a stunning, geological metaphor to illustrate the sheer weight and power of His revelation: "If We had sent down this Quran upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and split apart from the awe of Allah." Allah notes that He presents such parables to humanity so that they may deeply reflect.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: A mountain is the ultimate physical symbol of strength, stability, and unyielding hardness in the natural world. Yet, Allah reveals that even this colossal mass of stone would yield, crack, and crumble under the spiritual weight of the Quran. This parable is a sharp critique of the human heart. If a mountain would soften and shatter out of awe for God's words, how stubborn and locked must a human heart be to hear the same Quran recited and feel absolutely nothing? It challenges us to shatter our own internal "mountains" of pride and apathy.

verse_breakdowns.content_markdown:
The Surah reaches a glorious, symphonic climax by listing the beautiful, transcendent Names of Allah. He is introduced as:
• The Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, The Most Merciful (Ar-Rahman), The Especially Merciful (Ar-Raheem).
• The Sovereign (Al-Malik), The Holy (Al-Quddus), The Giver of Peace (Al-Salam), The Granter of Security (Al-Mu'min), The Guardian (Al-Muhaymin), The All-Mighty (Al-Aziz), The Compeller (Al-Jabbar), The Supreme (Al-Mutakabbir).
• The Creator (Al-Khaliq), The Inventor (Al-Bari), The Shaper (Al-Musawwir).
To Him belong the best names, and whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him, for He is the All-Mighty, the All-Wise.
verse_breakdowns.reflection: This closing passage is one of the most beloved and recited sequences in the Quran. It transitions beautifully from His absolute knowledge and mercy, to His political and spiritual sovereignty over the universe, and finally to His functional role as the artistic designer of creation. Understanding these Names is the key to deep Muraqabah (mindfulness); when we know Him as Al-Salam (the Source of Peace) and Al-Mu'min (the Giver of Security), we no longer seek sanctuary in the temporary "fortresses" of the physical world.

stories_in_surah.title: The Story Behind the Revelation: The Betrayal of Banu Nadir
stories_in_surah.content:
To fully grasp the verses of Surah Al-Hashr, one must understand the dramatic sequence of events that led to the military siege of the Banu Nadir fortress.

The Treaty and the Blood Money

When the Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) migrated to Madinah, he signed the Covenant of Madinah (Mithaq al-Madinah) with the Jewish tribes, including the Banu Nadir. This treaty guaranteed them religious freedom and protection in exchange for mutual defense and peaceful coexistence.

In the 4th year of Hijrah, a Muslim companion named Amr bin Umayyah accidentally killed two men from the Bani 'Amir tribe, with whom the Muslims had a peace treaty. The Prophet (pbuh) was legally obligated to pay the blood money (Diyah) to the victims' family.

Because the Banu Nadir were allies of both the Muslims and the Bani 'Amir, the Prophet (pbuh) walked to their settlement along with several close companions - including Abu Bakr, Umar, and Ali (ra) - to request their financial contribution toward the blood money, as dictated by the terms of their mutual treaty.

The Assassination Plot

The leaders of Banu Nadir pretended to cooperate, welcoming the Prophet (pbuh) and asking him to sit against the wall of one of their stone fortresses while they gathered the funds.

Behind closed doors, however, they conspired to assassinate him. They reasoned that they would never have a better opportunity to eliminate the leader of Islam. One of their men, Amr bin Jihash, volunteered to climb to the roof of the fortress and drop a massive stone millstone directly onto the Prophet's head.

The Divine Intervention

Before the conspirator could drop the stone, the Angel Gabriel (as) descended and informed the Prophet (pbuh) of the assassination plot. Acting calmly, the Prophet (pbuh) stood up as if to take care of a brief matter, walked away from the settlement, and immediately returned to Madinah.

When the companions realized he had left, they followed him back to the city. The Prophet (pbuh) informed them of the treachery. Because they had violated the foundational treaty of Madinah by attempting to assassinate the head of state, the Prophet (pbuh) sent them an ultimatum: they had ten days to leave Madinah with their possessions, or face military action.

The Siege and the Demolition of Homes

Initially, the Banu Nadir prepared to leave. However, Abdullah ibn Ubayy (the leader of the hypocrites in Madinah) sent them a message urging them to stay and fight, promising that he and his allies would stand by them.

Encouraged by this false promise, the Banu Nadir locked themselves in their highly fortified, stone castles, believing they were invincible. The Muslims marched out and laid siege to their fortresses.

During the siege, the Muslims cut down and burned some of the non-fruit-bearing date palm trees that surrounded the fortresses to clear their line of sight and break the enemy's morale. This caused great distress to the Banu Nadir, who accused the Prophet of causing corruption on earth. Allah vindicated the Muslims' actions in the Quran:

• "Whatever palm-trees you cut down or left standing upon their roots, it was by leave of Allah, and in order that He might disgrace the rebellious."* (Verse 5)

Realizing that the hypocrites would not help them and that their fortresses could not withstand the siege, the Banu Nadir surrendered after six days. They negotiated safe passage out of Madinah, allowed to carry only what could be loaded onto their camels.

In a display of spite and desperation, they did not want to leave their beautiful homes for the Muslims to enjoy. They began tearing down their own houses from the inside, ripping out valuable wooden doors, decorative beams, and window frames to pack onto their camels.

• "They demolished their own dwellings with their own hands and the hands of the believers. So take warning, O you who have eyes to see!"* (Verse 2)

deep_dives.title: The Legal Reform: The Concept of Fai' (Verses 6-10)
deep_dives.content:
Surah Al-Hashr introduced a groundbreaking legal distinction in Islamic jurisprudence regarding the wealth acquired from defeated hostile forces: the difference between Ghanimah and Fai'.

Distinguishing Ghanimah from *Fai'

• Ghanimah (Spoils of War): Booty acquired through physical combat, where Muslim soldiers risked their lives on horses and camels. Under Islamic law (Surah Al-Anfal), four-fifths (80%) of Ghanimah is distributed directly among the fighting soldiers, while one-fifth (20%) is reserved for the state.
• Fai' (Peaceful Acquisition): Wealth, land, or property acquired from an enemy without actual physical combat or active military engagement. Because the Banu Nadir surrendered without a full-scale battle, their vast properties and date groves were classified as Fai'.

The Divine Distribution of *Fai'

Allah decreed that because the soldiers did not have to charge their horses or camels to win this wealth, they had no automatic right to share it. Instead, the distribution of Fai' was given entirely to the Prophet (pbuh) to allocate according to divine guidelines:

• "And what Allah restored [of property] to His Messenger from them - you did not spur for it any horses or camels, but Allah gives His messengers power over whom He wills..."* (Verse 6)

Allah specified that Fai' belongs to:

1. Allah and His Messenger (for state administrative and defense costs)
2. The Prophet's close relatives (who were legally barred from receiving charity/Zakat)
3. Orphans
4. The needy
5. Wayfarers (stranded travelers)

The Economic Philosophy of Islam

In Verse 7, Allah explains the profound social and economic wisdom behind this distribution method:

• ".so that it does not remain circulating among your rich people only."* (Verse 7)

This is one of the most vital economic principles in the Quran. It establishes that Islam is fundamentally opposed to the hyper-concentration of wealth. Capital must flow dynamically through society, reaching the lowest social strata to prevent the creation of an oligarchic class structure where the rich control all resources while the poor remain permanently marginalized.

deep_dives.title: The Social Portrait: Emigrants, Helpers, and the Generations to Come
deep_dives.content:
In verses 8 through 10, Allah paints a beautiful, timeless portrait of the Islamic community, dividing them into three distinct groups based on their historical roles and spiritual sincerity.

Group 1: The Muhajirun (The Emigrants)

These were the early Muslims of Makkah who sacrificed everything for the sake of Islam:

• "For the poor emigrants who were expelled from their homes and their properties, seeking bounty from Allah and [His] approval and supporting Allah and His Messenger. Those are the truthful."* (Verse 8)

The Prophet (pbuh) utilized the Fai' acquired from the Banu Nadir to solve a major socioeconomic crisis in Madinah. Up to this point, the Muhajirun had been living as guests in the homes of the local Madinans, owning no land or businesses of their own. By distributing the lands of Banu Nadir almost exclusively to the poor Muhajirun, the Prophet (pbuh) made them financially independent, easing the burden on the hosts and integrating them fully into the Madinan economy.

Group 2: The Ansar (The Helpers)

Allah praises the local helpers of Madinah for their unmatched generosity, hospitality, and lack of jealousy:

• "And [also for] those who were settled in the Home [i.e., Madinah] and [adopted] the faith before them. They love those who emigrated to them and find not any jealousy in their chests of what the emigrants were given, but give them preference over themselves, even though they are in privation."* (Verse 9)

When the lands of Banu Nadir were given to the Muhajirun, the Ansar did not complain. Instead, they celebrated that their brothers had finally secured homes and livelihoods. This verse praises their Eethar (altruism) - the noble spiritual quality of prioritizing others over oneself, even in times of personal poverty.

Group 3: The Successors (Those Who Came After)

This group represents every Muslim who entered Islam after the initial generation, extending all the way to the Day of Judgment:

• "And [also for] those who came after them, saying, 'Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith and put not in our hearts any resentment toward those who have believed. Our Lord, indeed You are Kind and Merciful.'"* (Verse 10)

This verse establishes that a defining characteristic of a true believer is a heart clean of malice, envy, or hatred toward any other Muslim, coupled with a deep respect and prayer of forgiveness for the righteous predecessors who preserved the faith for future generations.

deep_dives.title: The Psychology of Hypocrisy (Verses 11-17)
deep_dives.content:
Surah Al-Hashr dedicates a significant section to exposing the hollow promises, cowardice, and internal division of the hypocrites (Munafiqun) led by Abdullah ibn Ubayy.

The Broken Promises

The hypocrites secretly reached out to the Banu Nadir and promised them:

• "If you are expelled, we will surely leave with you, and we will never obey anyone concerning you... and if you are fought, we will surely aid you."* (Verse 11)

Allah exposed this as a flat-out lie, predicting exactly how they would behave when the siege actually began:

• If the Banu Nadir were expelled, the hypocrites would not pack up and leave with them.
• If they were fought, the hypocrites would not help them.
• Even if they did try to offer nominal help, they would quickly turn their backs and flee in cowardice.

The Illusion of Unity

To the outward observer, the alliance of the hypocrites and their co-conspirators looked strong. However, Allah revealed their internal reality:

• "You think they are together, but their hearts are diverse. That is because they are a people who do not reason."* (Verse 14)

They were united only by temporary self-interest, fear, and shared hatred - not by any shared moral or spiritual principles. Because of this, their alliances collapsed the moment they faced actual pressure.

The Parable of Satan

Allah compares the way the hypocrites lured the Banu Nadir into ruin to the deceitful tactics of Satan:

• "Like the example of Satan when he says to man, 'Disbelieve.' But when he disbelieves, he says, 'Indeed, I am disassociated from you. Indeed, I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds.'"* (Verse 16)

Abdullah ibn Ubayy pushed the Banu Nadir to fight, but the moment the Muslims marched out, he abandoned them completely to face their exile alone.

deep_dives.title: The Ultimate Greatness: The Power of the Quran and the Names of Allah
deep_dives.content:
The Surah concludes with a breathtaking transition from political, historical, and legislative matters to the absolute spiritual majesty of the Creator.

The Parable of the Mountain

To remind humanity of the sheer weight and transformative power of the revelation they take for granted, Allah states:

• "Had We sent down this Quran upon a mountain, you would have seen it humbled and splitting asunder from the fear of Allah. And these examples We present to the people that perhaps they will give thought."* (Verse 21)

If a massive, solid, unyielding stone mountain possessed consciousness, it would crumble into dust out of awe and reverence for Allah's words. Yet, human beings often receive the Quran with hardened hearts, unaffected by its warnings and promises.

The Beautiful Names of Allah (Verses 22-24)

The final three verses of Surah Al-Hashr contain one of the most comprehensive and beautiful concentrations of Divine Names and Attributes in the entire Quran, establishing His absolute power, mercy, and perfection.

• The Sovereign and Holy: He is Al-Malik (The Supreme King), Al-Quddus (The Holy, free of all defects), and Al-Salam (The Source of Peace).
• The Protector and Almighty: He is Al-Mu'min (The Giver of Security), Al-Muhaymin (The Guardian over all), Al-Aziz (The Almighty), Al-Jabbar (The Compeller), and Al-Mutakabbir (The Supreme in Majesty).
• The Creator and Fashioner: He is Al-Khaliq (The Creator), Al-Bari' (The Producer from nothing), and Al-Musawwir (The Fashioner of forms and beauty).

• Hadith Context on the Last Three Verses:* Ma'qil ibn Yasar (ra) narrated that the Prophet (pbuh) said: "Whoever says three times in the morning: 'A'udhu billahis-Sami'il-'Alimi minash-Shaytanir-rajim' (I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan) and then recites the last three verses of Surah Al-Hashr, Allah will appoint seventy thousand angels to pray for him until the evening. If he dies on that day, he dies as a martyr. And whoever recites them in the evening will reach the same status." (Sunan al-Tirmidhi, graded Hasan)

deep_dives.title: Summary of Lessons
deep_dives.content:
Surah Al-Hashr teaches the early Muslim community and all generations that follow several eternal truths:

1. Invincibility Belongs Only to God: The Banu Nadir believed their physical fortresses, wealth, and alliances made them secure, but these crumbled instantly when they betrayed their moral covenants.
2. Equity is the Heart of Islamic Finance: The legislation of Fai' ensures that society's surplus wealth is distributed to the vulnerable, rather than remaining locked in a cycle of wealth concentration among the elite.
3. True Unity is Spiritual, Not Tactical: True brotherhood is built on love, selfless sacrifice (Eethar), and clean hearts (like the Muhajirun and Ansar), while alliances based on hypocrisy, greed, and spite are structurally hollow and bound to fail.
